Triggers.value: Water, flooding, or large bodies of water

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

vignette: The night his younger brother, David, vanished during the basement flood remains etched in Professor Amari Okafor’s memory not as a sequence of events, but as a suffocating certainty. The rain had hammered against the roof for hours before the sump pump failed, turning their shared study into a churning lake of dark water and splintered drywall. Amari had reached the top of the stairs just as the current pulled David under, leaving him with nothing but the sharp, chemical tang of wet insulation and the sound of his brother’s last exhale swallowed by the rising tide. At fifty-nine, living alone in a city that now feels too heavy with rain, he carries the weight of that single moment, and what frightened him most was the helplessness of watching the water claim someone he loved. Over the weeks that followed, that damp, metallic scent began to hijack his nervous system. Now, a simple drop of rain against his department office window or the whiff of wet wool from a colleague’s coat sends his pulse racing before his conscious mind can register the source. He was certain that the danger was returning the instant those cues appeared, his chest tightening and his hands trembling as a wave of horror and guilt flooded him. He cannot sit through a lecture without scanning the ceiling for leaks, his body bracing for a disaster that is not happening. The moment the water surfaces, or even the ghost of that basement odor crosses his path, it pulls him into a paroxysm of dread that leaves him unable to relax even when he knows he is behind locked doors. He had come to believe that his own physiology was betraying him, turning everyday dampness into an immediate threat. That relentless physiological alertness, in turn, narrows his attention until nothing else exists. Because his system stays locked in survival mode, he finds himself scanning every environment for signs of rising water or mounting pressure, effectively manufacturing the very triggers he fears. When departmental stress climbs during grant deadlines, his shoulders lock and his breath shallows, causing him to fixate on the nearby campus rain garden until he must excuse himself. The more his body reacts to imagined danger before he has even had time to think, the more sharply he detects water and stress in his periphery, turning his own hypervigilance into a self-reinforcing warning system. This tightening loop has fundamentally altered his daily life as a professor; he has cancelled all off-site symposia and stopped supervising graduate students who propose water-related research, claiming he can no longer manage unpredictability. His colleagues notice the distance, but he is too occupied with muting sudden spikes of shame to explain himself. What finally brought him to seek help was a trembling episode during a mid-semester lecture when the building’s HVAC system kicked on, spraying a fine mist that triggered a full panic response in the front row. He stands now in the quiet of my office, not sure if he wants to forget the night David vanished, but desperate to stop his own body from betraying him every time the sky turns heavy.
